posts.title: Tired ad or slow starter: reading fatigue from history
posts.hook: Tired ads and slow starters look the same on a cost chart.
posts.caption:
Tired ads and slow starters look the same on a cost chart.
One needs a new opening. The other needs you to leave it alone.

Both show a cost per order above your account average, so the cost column cannot separate them.

History can. An ad can only be tired if it was once good.

In Galvor's analysis of video ads launched May to September 2026, some ad styles started about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and ended close to average over their life. Cut those in week one and you never see the second half.

Swipe for the order I check things in, and the four calls it leads to.

posts.title: Poll: which kind of new ad got more first-month spend
posts.hook: Three kinds of new ad. Only one got more spend.
posts.caption:
Three kinds of new ad. Only one got more spend.
Your next brief probably contains all three.

We took every new video ad launched from May to September 2026 across the brands we work with, and looked at how much spend each one got in its first month.

Then we sorted them into three kinds.

A. A proven message, shot in a new look.
B. A new message, over a familiar first shot.
C. A new ad that looks like many ads already running.

One kind got clearly more first-month spend. The other two got less.

It matters this week because sale season has just ended, and December briefs tend to be written from the looks that are already in the account.

Vote below. I will post the answer, with the numbers, in the comments tomorrow.

posts.title: Rank ads on orders that stayed, not orders placed
posts.hook: The ad with the cheapest orders can be your most expensive ad.
posts.caption:
The ad with the cheapest orders can be your most expensive ad.
Ads Manager counts an order when it is placed. Your bank counts it when it is delivered and kept.

For an Indian D2C brand selling cash on delivery, a lot can happen in between. The parcel is refused at the door, or it comes back a week later.

Meta sees none of that. It keeps finding more people like the ones who placed the order.

Here is the check I would run before the next budget review.

1. Export orders by ad for a month that has fully closed, so deliveries and returns have settled.

2. Join each order to its final status: kept, refused or returned.

3. Work out cost per order again, counting kept orders only.

4. Rank the ads again.

Then look at which ads moved. If one drops several places, watch its opening. An offer-led hook and a problem-led hook can bring very different buyers at the same cost per order.

The ad decides who shows up. Rank it on the orders that stayed.

posts.title: The four-call test for every chart in a weekly review
posts.hook: A chart that cannot change a decision is decoration.
posts.caption:
A chart that cannot change a decision is decoration.
I use that as a build rule. You can use it on your own weekly ad review.

Take the deck or dashboard your team opens every Monday. For each chart, ask which of four calls it could change.

Scale this ad.
Cut this ad.
Refresh this ad.
Test something new.

If the answer is none, the chart is reporting. Reporting is fine in a monthly note. In a weekly review it eats the minutes you needed for the real argument: why did that ad do well, and what do we make next?

This is the rule we build to at Galvor. A screen has to end in one of those four words. If we cannot say which one, the screen is not finished.

Two views usually pass the test. Cost per order by ad. And what your good ads have in common. Blended account averages usually fail it, because an average cannot tell you which ad to touch.

Try it on Monday. Count the charts, then count the decisions.

posts.title: Where the human stands: three questions before you trust an agent
posts.hook: Our AI co-worker can recommend a budget move. It cannot make one.
posts.caption:
Our AI co-worker can recommend a budget move. It cannot make one.
That was a design choice, and I would make it again.

The fair doubt about any agent in a marketing team is simple: what happens when it is wrong?

My answer is to decide, before building anything, where a person stands. Three questions sort it.

Can the mistake be undone for free? A wrong tag on an ad can. Let the system act, and review in bulk.

Does the mistake spend money? A budget shift does. The system shows its reasoning and a person approves. Galvor never touches the media budget.

Could the mistake hurt the brand? A claim in a script could. A person reads it before it goes anywhere.

The engineering work is making that review quick: the recommendation, the evidence and the expected result in one place. Someone who can see why can say yes or no in a couple of minutes.

If you are evaluating an agent this quarter, ask the vendor to draw this map. Where does it act alone, and where does it wait?

An agent you can overrule is one you can let near real money.

posts.title: Ad of the Week #2: log the first three seconds in four fields
posts.hook: Hook rate says an opening worked. It cannot say why.
posts.caption:
Hook rate says an opening worked. It cannot say why.
The first three seconds can, if you write them down the same way every time.

Ad of the Week #2 is a method, shown on a made-up example: a festive gifting ad for a tea brand. No real brand and no real numbers.

I log four things about the opening of an ad. What is in the first frame. What the first words promise. Who is on screen. When the product shows up.

Same four fields, same order, every ad. After twenty ads you can sort the sheet and see which kind of opening your good ads share.

A quiet week is a good time to log this year's ads.

posts.title: Four questions for any agent that 'learns from its mistakes'
posts.hook: 'Our agent learns from its mistakes' should make you ask one thing.
posts.caption:
'Our agent learns from its mistakes' should make you ask one thing.
What did it write down before the mistake?

Learning needs a record. Without one, an agent that changes its behaviour is only drifting. These are the four questions I would put to any vendor, and the standard we hold our own work to.

1. Does each recommendation record what it expected? 'Scale this ad' is a guess until it says what should happen, and by when.

2. Is it scored against what happened? A recommendation nobody scores is an opinion.

3. When it was wrong, can it tell thin data from bad reasoning? An ad with too few orders teaches nothing. That miss should be flagged and left alone.

4. Who approves a change to the rules? An agent that quietly rewrites itself is an agent nobody can audit. A person should see the miss first.

None of this is clever. It is bookkeeping: a prediction, a result and a note on the gap, kept for every call.

In a Monday review, that is what learning should look like. You open the record and see where the system was wrong.

posts.title: Ad of the Week #3: in a gifting ad, write the hook for the giver
posts.hook: In a gifting ad, the buyer and the user are different people.
posts.caption:
In a gifting ad, the buyer and the user are different people.
That changes who the first three seconds should talk to.

Ad of the Week #3 is a pattern, shown on a made-up example: a gifting ad for a candle brand. No real brand and no real results.

A normal product ad answers 'do I want this?'. A gifting ad has to answer the giver's question: 'will they like it, and will it look like I thought about it?'

So the opening names the person receiving the gift. The product arrives as the answer. The giver's worries get handled before the price.

Valentine's briefs get written this month. Swipe for the structure, and one caution from our data.

posts.title: Same category, three hooks: a 20-minute Ad Library exercise
posts.hook: Line up three ads from your category. Read only the openings.
posts.caption:
Line up three ads from your category. Read only the openings.
What they share tells you where your next ad will blend in.

This is a 20-minute exercise with the public Meta Ad Library. I have shown it on a made-up set of three sunscreen ads, so no real brand is being judged.

Sort each opening into one of three lanes. It opens on a problem, on proof, or on a person. Then count.

One caution on what the count means. The library shows what a brand is running. It does not show what is selling. So a crowded lane is a fact about the feed.

The empty lane is a test worth running on your own ads.

posts.title: Ad of the Week #4: the sale ad that opens without the discount
posts.hook: During a sale, the discount is the one thing every ad shares.
posts.caption:
During a sale, the discount is the one thing every ad shares.
So it is the weakest thing to open with.

Ad of the Week #4 is a pattern from sale season, shown on a made-up Republic Day ad for a cookware brand. No real brand and no real results.

The structure: open on the reason to want the product, show it doing its job, then land the offer as the reason to act today.

There is a delivery reason too. In Galvor's analysis of new video ads launched May to September 2026, six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less first-month spend. Sale week is when teams launch six versions of one banner.

posts.title: Hook teardown: the delete test
posts.hook: A hook that stops the scroll can still lose the sale.
posts.caption:
A hook that stops the scroll can still lose the sale.
Its second job is to set up the next shot, and that job is easy to skip.

There is a quick test for it. Delete the first three seconds of your ad and play the rest. If the ad still makes complete sense, nothing after the hook needed it. The hook was decoration.

In your numbers this can show up as a healthy hook rate with a weak hold rate. People stop, then leave.

The fix in the video is small. Write the hook as a question that the second shot has to answer, with the product in the answer.

The example is a made-up ad, drawn as a storyboard. No real brand.

Video below, 43 seconds.

posts.title: Five things our ad data showed in 2026, each with its number
posts.hook: Five things our ad data showed in 2026. Each with its number.
posts.caption:
Five things our ad data showed in 2026. Each with its number.
All five come from Galvor's analysis of ads launched from May to September across the brands we work with.

The short version: Meta's delivery now favours an ad that looks different from what you already run, and some ad styles need longer before you judge them.

Two limits. The analysis covers brands we work with, so treat each finding as a pattern to test in your own account. And four of the five are about spend and cost in the early weeks, which is delivery. Whether an ad sells over its life is a separate question.

Swipe for the five.
posts.alt_text: Eight-slide carousel. Cover: Five things the ads told us in 2026. Then five stat slides: new ads that looked like many running ads got 36 percent less first-month spend; a proven message in a new look got 47 percent more; six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48 percent less; some ad styles start 35 percent dearer per order in the first two months; one brand's creative diversity score went from 63 to 92 out of 100. Then four moves for this quarter and a closing slide asking readers to follow Galvor.

posts.title: A long-running ad proves only that nobody switched it off
posts.hook: A long-running ad has proved one thing: nobody switched it off.
posts.caption:
A long-running ad has proved one thing: nobody switched it off.
That is all the Meta Ad Library can tell you about it.

It happens in most competitor reviews. Someone finds an ad that has been live for 60 days, and the room decides it must be working.

The library shows that an ad is active and when it started. It does not show budget, results, or whether the ad sits in a test or a scaling campaign. An ad can stay live because it sells, because it is cheap to leave on, or because nobody tidied the account.

So I treat the duration as a question, and look for three things around it.

1. Versions. Did new cuts of the same ad appear over time? Then someone is still investing in it.

2. What stayed fixed. If the opening holds while the offer and the ending change, the opening is the part they trust.

3. What stopped. Similar ads from the same brand that ended early tell you more than the one that survived.

Even then, what you have is a guess about their ad. The proof can only come from a test in your own account.

It is why we never state a competitor's results from public data.
